https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-.text: KYIV — Ukraine faces a €23 billion hole in its defense budget this year, leaving Kyiv scrambling for cash to fight Russia even as Western leaders gathered in the capital to mark the country's independence day and pledge ongoing support. The money is needed not only for weapons and air defense, but also to pay soldiers, support the families of those killed and ensure Ukraine has the supplies it needs to start 2027. “We are not asking [you] to fight for us. Give Ukraine everything to stop this war, to stop it faster than Putin can start the next one,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a speech Monday. Advertisement Advertisement U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was in Kyiv Monday for a meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing. European Council President António Costa, Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Estonian President Alar Karis, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also attended in person, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joined remotely. “Ukrainian people deserve not just continued support but our gratitude ... I am determined we [the coalition of the willing] will work together to deliver the support you need,” Burnham said in a statement. The funding gap originated after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of the year, while the EU’s €90 billion loan was delayed by roadblocks from Hungary. “At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half," Zelenskyy said during a meeting with reporters on Saturday. The shortfall comes on top of €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan. Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June. Advertisement Advertisement "Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented,” Zelenskyy added. The European Commission offered some relief Monday, approving €6.1 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine. This latest disbursement from the EU’s €90 billion loan package will fund air-defense missiles and ammunition, as well as radars — among Kyiv’s most urgent needs. But the money falls far short of what Ukraine says it requires. Ukraine needs about €6.8 billion to €8.5 billion to ensure a “normal start” to next year, the Ukrainian leader said. That money is effectively needed in advance to pay for weapons and other supplies for January 2027. Around €17 billion more is needed for military salaries, payments to the families of fallen soldiers and other expenses. “A lot of money is needed,” he added. But domestic politics are also creating obstacles to international funding. Zelenskyy admitted that Ukrainian lawmakers are stalling the implementation of reforms on which some international aid is conditional. Overall, parliament is currently delaying 24 reform bills tied to Western funding disbursement. While not all the funds are tied to defense spending, getting EU money would free up Ukraine's scarce resources for other urgent defense needs. Advertisement Advertisement Last week, the Ukrainian parliament’s law enforcement committee removed five government and judicial reform bills from consideration because they are no longer relevant, Ukrainian MP Anastasiya Radina said last week. Maksym Buzhanskiy, a lawmaker from Zelenskyy's party, defended the committee's decision to remove the bills, claiming they do not correspond to Ukraine commitments needed for EU funding. Zelenskyy is planning to ask for disbursement of EU funds ahead of schedule. “I am working on this with the French and the Germans. Practically, we need to bring forward the second portion of the European funds allocated for Ukraine, and this is an extremely difficult task,” Zelenskyy said.

https://whbl.com/2026/09/22/estonia-says.text: Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER EVENTS OBITUARIES CLOSINGS MORE AGRICULTURE BLOGS LOCAL SPORTS ON AIR PODCASTS Estonia says France must explain push to lift EU sanctions on Usmanov By Thomson Reuters Sep 22, 2026 | 5:20 PM By John Irish UNITED NATIONS, Sept 22 (Reuters) – France should explain itself after it pushed for the lifting of EU sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov, Estonia’s foreign minister said ​on Tuesday, describing the move as sending the wrong signal ‌at the wrong time. European Union envoys agreed on Tuesday to drop two high-profile billionaires, Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the EU’s Russian sanctions list in a compromise deal to renew sanctions on roughly 3,000 other listed individuals and entities. Earlier ‌this ​month, France shocked other EU members when ⁠it pushed for Russian-Uzbek ⁠metals tycoon Usmanov to be removed from EU sanctions, citing national security concerns. “One country put a very strong position on the table that these two people must be delisted, otherwise we’re actually ​losing the sanctions regime,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Reuters in an interview on the sidelines of the United Nations General ⁠Assembly. “This is a totally wrong message.” “They need ⁠to explain themselves. There was no deep explanation,” ​he said. France came under pressure from Azerbaijan, where at least two French ​nationals are detained, three European diplomats told Reuters last week. They ‌added that Paris had indicated in private that Baku was using Usmanov to “blackmail” it over the case of two French citizens held in Azerbaijan, an assertion rejected by Baku. But there has been no ⁠public comment by the French presidency, which diplomats said had taken the lead on the dossier. Usmanov has long been associated with luxury assets in ⁠Western Europe, including property ‌on the French Riviera, and was placed under ⁠EU sanctions in 2022 as one of Russia’s ​wealthiest ‌businessmen. Multiple European officials said France’s position had left ​them perplexed, hurt ⁠Paris’ credibility and roiled efforts to present a united European front against Russia. “The delisting is sending a very bad signal at a very wrong time when Russia is actually putting more pressure on Ukraine and attacking the civil infrastructure people,” he said. https://telex.hu/karakter/kultura/2026/1.text: Menü Kereső Lengyel Tamás: A fideszes maffiaállamnak nemcsak áldozatai, hanem okai is vagyunk Kultúra Lengyel Tamás és Krug Emília a Szinten túl című műsorban – Forrás: Szinten túl / YouTube Rácz Attila „Mit lehet csinálni, amikor egy nagy film, mondjuk a Most vagy soha!, elviszi a magyar filmre fordítandó keretösszeg egyharmadát, a kétharmadát pedig elviszi a Hunyadi-film? […] Kispadon ültek a jobbnál jobb alkotók. Hajdu Szabolcs is fillérekből és szívességi alapon forgatott. Szerintem ez a rendszernek lett egyszer csak a következménye” – mondta Lengyel Tamás színész a Szinten túl Krug Emíliával legutóbbi adásában. A beszélgetés apropója a Tasnádi István által rendezett, független produkcióként készült, október 22-én bemutatásra kerülő Örökség című film volt, és Lengyel annak kapcsán fogalmazott így, hogy a színészek – Lengyel mellett Mucsi Zoltán és Molnár Áron – ingyen dolgoztak a filmen, a forgatásra pedig 14 nap állt rendelkezésre, holott általában harminc-negyven nap alatt vesznek fel egy ilyen alkotást. „Én biztos, hogy nem költenék hétmilliárd forintot egy filmre. Azt hiszem, hogy csinálnék egy pályázatot, ahol lehet pályázni, és azok az emberek, akik nem részesültek támogatásban, szakmai alapon hozzá tudnának jutni. Felosztanám ezt a hétmilliárdot hét egymilliárdos összegre vagy tíz hétszázmilliósra” – mondta a színész arról, hogy milyen filmtámogatási rendszert tartana igazságosabbnak. Lengyel a Loupe Színházi Társulás tagjaként arról is beszélt, hogy mivel a társulatnak van lehetősége a piacról megélni, nem fognak pályázni olyan állami forrásokra, amelyek színházcsinálásra vannak fenntartva. „Nem fogunk pályázni, hogy ne vegyük el a pénzt, a lehetőséget azoktól, akik ismertség hiányában nem tudnak ilyen nézettségre szert tenni, mint amire mi. [...] 9,5 millióan élünk itt, Magyarországon. Ez egy olyan piac, ami sok független dolgot nem tud eltartani.” Lengyel arra is kitért, hogy szerinte létre kellene hozni egy színészkamarát, és előírná, hogy minden olyan produkcióban, amiben közpénz van, a résztvevők 70 százalékának kamarai tagnak kellene lennie. „Őszintén szólva már nem hiszek abban, hogy alulról meg tud szerveződni egy érdekképviselet a színészek körében. Egyszerűen kizártnak tartom. Azt gondolom, hogy felelős embereknek meg kell hozni azokat a döntéseket, amik aztán ennek a szakmai közösségnek jók lesznek. Ezt a szabályrendszert fönt kell megalkotni. [...] Azt érzem, hogy nagyon alacsony a képességünk a szerveződésre” – fogalmazott szkeptikusan. A színész arról a félelméről is beszélt, hogy hiába cserélik le a kulturális elit fejét, „ugyanolyan kizárólagosságban” fognak megtörténni a döntések, mint eddig. „Hogy lehet, hogy Kiss-B. Atilla idén megint osztályt indított az SZFE-n, miközben április 12-én volt egy rendszerváltás? [...] Hogy lehet, hogy amikor van egy kormányváltás, akkor nem az az első, hogy azokat a problémás embereket, akiknek az ügye nem került kivizsgálásra, kivesszük a rendszerből, amíg nem születik róluk mondás vagy ítélet?” – mondta Lengyel, aki szerint összecsúsznak a rendszerek, és továbbra is hatékonyan működnek az érdeklobbik. A beszélgetés során szóba került az Eszenyi-ügy és Máté Gábor Ördögkatlanon elhangzott , nagy visszhangot kiváltó véleménye is. Erről Lengyel most azt mondta: „Azért tartom veszélyesnek az olyan jellegű kijelentéseket, mint amiket Máté Gábor tett, mert a következményekre irányuló igényt szünteti meg, vagy annullálja. Egy idő után, amikor az ember ezt sokat hangoztatja, hogy dehát nem volt következménye, meg nem kért bocsánatot, már úgy érzi, hogy ezt fölösleges elmondani ennyiszer. [...] Én akkor éreznék befejezettnek egy ilyet, hogy ha felállna egy független etikai bizottság, amiben sokféle ember van, akik nincsenek az aktuális hatalomtól és a szakmában diszponáló emberektől függő viszonyban, hanem egy teljesen külső bizottság. [...] Most mi történik, ha valakiről megállapítják ebben a szakmában, hogy bántalmazó volt? Attól ő ugyanúgy tud dolgozni. Az intézmények vagy a szerveződések elhatárolódhatnak tőle, de erre nincs semmiféle szabályrendszer kialakítva. Ezt meg kéne szülni, valahogy létre kellene hozni.” Lengyel az elszámoltatás kérdésével kapcsolatban úgy fogalmazott: „Meg kell értenünk, hogy mi történt a társadalomban az elmúlt tizenhat évben, elemezni kell, fel kell rajzolni, rá kell tenni egy térképre, hogy hogyan juthattunk el ehhez a tizenhat évhez, ami megtörtént közöttünk. Az elszámoltatást pedig normális jogi úton kell végrehajtani, demokratikus keretek között.” A színész szerint ha az emberek egyszer csak azt tapasztalják, hogy megszűnik a következménynélküliség, az nyugalmat fog hozni a társadalomban. „Meggyőződésem, hogy ha egy Fidesz-szavazó azt fogja érzékelni, hogy milyen mennyiségű volt az a pénz, amit kiloptak ebből az országból, és azt nem ennek az országnak fejlődésére, megváltoztatására használtak fel, ugyanúgy egyet fog ezzel érteni.” A beszélgetés végén a műsorvezető arra volt kíváncsi, Lengyel mennyire megbocsátó azokkal, akik együttműködtek a NER-rel. „Az elmúlt tizenhat évben az egy probléma volt, hogy nem mondtuk azt dolgokra, hogy nem. Bizonyos oldalról megértem ezt az egzisztenciális kérdést. [...] Nem feltétlenül ítélem el azokat az embereket, akik a Hunyadi című izében szerepeltek, de az már biztosan nem esik jól, hogy kritikamentesen gondolkodnak a filmalkotásról” – válaszolta a színész, aki saját bevallása szerint bizonyos kérdésekben radikálisan gondolkodik, más kérdésekben viszont megbocsátóbb ebben a témában. „De összességében az, hogy tizenhat évig uralkodott rajtunk egy ilyen maffiaállam, és kirabolta még a padlást is, annak nemcsak az áldozatai vagyunk, hanem az okai is. Hát mi nem léptünk fel ellene” – mondta Lengyel Tamás a Szinten túl legutóbbi adásában. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

https://www.eldoradonews.com/news/2026/o.text: Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia put on hold by Trump KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in favor of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order putting the sweeping restrictions on hold. The White House decision has heightened fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow's escalating attacks as winter approaches. Overnight Russian attacks killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities. In a social media statement, Zelenskyy called Trump's decision unfortunate but avoided directly criticizing the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days. "A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters." He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, saying that blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing and that limiting Ukraine's ability to retaliate would not bring peace. "Nevertheless, we very much hope -- and I personally hope -- that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he said. Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, had met Friday with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. Zelenskyy said the U.S. was working to arrange a three-way meeting involving him, Trump and Putin, potentially in the Middle East, Europe or the United States. Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving. Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. Trump told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, criticized Trump's move, saying the president was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies." "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said. Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine. Republicans and Democrats alike say the purchase will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran. Starlink restrictions were planned, Zelenskyy says Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was investigating sudden speed restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. The restrictions, imposed without warning early Thursday, cut the internet data connection when a communication terminal moves faster than 160 kph (100 mph). The cap forced Ukrainian drones to fly slower than usual, making it easier for Russian weapons to target or evade them. Zelenskyy said that there were no similar restrictions in European Union countries and that they apply only to Ukraine. "In other words, this is a planned operation," he said. It was unclear who was responsible. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. The Pentagon has not answered questions from The Associated Press about the restrictions. Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions on the system. He also doubted that the disruption came from Musk. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Kyiv reports a 'massive' energy strike Moscow carried out a massive strike on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country, Zelenskyy said. "The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia's strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences," he said. Ukraine's air force said it intercepted all four of Russia's cruise missiles and most of the 332 attack drones it fired overnight. Russia's heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine's appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months. Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine's Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, wounded at least 33 others, he said. Ukrainian drones disrupt Moscow airports A Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said. Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones. The Kremlin announced Saturday that Putin approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks Romania downs 2 drones over Black Sea Romania's Ministry of National Defense said Saturday that its pilots had shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters in the Black Sea. Two F-16s were scrambled at 5:43 p.m. local time after radar systems "detected a group of aerial targets moving southwest, approximately 120 kilometers east of Snake Island," the ministry said. The drones entered the NATO member's airspace around 6 p.m. and were shot down minutes later. "Both aerial targets were identified as drones and were shot down over Romania's territorial waters," the ministry said. It later identified the drones as jet-powered and from "Geran family," which are types of drones Moscow has used in Ukraine. The incident follows a spate of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels off the Black Sea coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in October. Scores of drones have crossed into Romanian airspace over the past two years, with officials attributing many of the incursions to Russia. Romania first shot down drones this year, marking its first such action since Moscow invaded neighboring Ukraine. You're one step away from the full story. https://www.ecoticias.com/en/psychology-.text: Science Psychology says suppressing thoughts doesn’t have to backfire the way a famous 1987 white bear experiment suggested, and a new study found the expected rebound never showed up By Adrian Villellas Published On: November 4, 2026 at 6:30 PM Add as preferred source Add ECOticias as a preferred source on Google × Share this story Copy link Link copied Psychology says suppressing thoughts may work better than its most famous experiment suggests. Aneta Niczyporuk of the University of Bialystok in Poland retested the classic white bear task. Her study, published online on September 22, 2026, found no sign that pushed-away thoughts came back stronger. The paper in Consciousness and Cognition reports that suppression worked while people were doing it. A Bayesian analysis weighs how well data support rival explanations. Here it gave strong evidence that the later rebound never happened. Five minutes with a bell The idea goes back to a 1987 paper by psychologist Daniel Wegner and three colleagues. Volunteers spoke their stream of consciousness aloud for five minutes. All the while, they tried not to think of a white bear. Each time the animal slipped into mind, they rang a bell. Both the bell rings and the spoken mentions told the same story. According to the paper, people “were unable to suppress the thought as instructed.” Then came the twist that made the study famous. When the same volunteers were asked to think about the bear for five minutes, they produced more bear thoughts than people told to think about it from the start. A second experiment gave some volunteers a specific distracter thought, and they were less likely to dwell on the bear later. Psychologists gave that later jump a name, the rebound effect. Wegner’s team wrote that suppression might even produce “the very obsession or preoccupation that it is directed against.” Many people know that struggle from replaying a conversation in their head . Wegner explains the bear The bear itself came from a novelist. Niczyporuk’s review traces it to Fyodor Dostoevsky, who described trying not to think of a polar bear. About 100 years later, that example inspired the first lab test. In 1994 Wegner offered an explanation he called ironic process theory. Any attempt at mental control, he proposed, starts two processes. One hunts for distractions, and the other keeps checking whether the forbidden thought is back. As long as the distraction search keeps running, attention stays away from the forbidden thought, according to Niczyporuk’s review. When that search stops, either because the effort ends or because mental resources run short , the theory expects a rebound. The checker keeps the unwanted idea easy to reach. Bialystok finds no rebound Niczyporuk set out to test both the task and the theory behind it. She added a preliminary phase before the suppression phase. Earlier studies, she writes, “often” left that step out. Her abstract is blunt about the outcome: “No paradoxical effects were found.” Ironic process theory predicts that suppressed thoughts become more accessible, and that did not happen either. She also measured how easily the target content came to mind. Those scores had no link with how often people reported the thought. The theory treats the two as parts of one mechanism. The three phases of a typical white bear experiment, with an experimental group told not to think of a white bear and a control group free to think of anything. (Image: Aneta Niczyporuk / Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, CC BY 4.0) Motivation may explain the old results Instead of an ironic mental monitor, the paper points to motivation. The abstract says the outcomes of the white bear task “were better accounted for by motivational factors.” Niczyporuk laid out the worry in a December 2025 review in Psychonomic Bulletin & Review . The task relies on people reporting their own thoughts. That count may shift with their wish to do well, or with simple resistance to being told what to do. Volunteers may also read the instruction differently, Niczyporuk notes. Does a white bear thought mean a detailed image of the animal’s teeth? Or does a quick memory of the instruction count too? Thirty-one studies and a bias Earlier meta-analyses had sided with Wegner. A 2020 meta-analysis by Deming Adam Wang and colleagues pooled 31 studies. It found rebound effects regardless of cognitive load. That same analysis also detected a small-study bias. In this pattern, smaller experiments tend to report bigger effects. Niczyporuk’s review notes that once the bias was corrected, the rebound was no longer statistically significant. Her review also counts how often the effect ran backward. In the meta-analyses she examined, the rebound reversed in 18 percent to 46 percent of the cases. A different lab method, the think/no-think paradigm, points the same way. Volunteers learn word pairs, then see a cue and either recall the partner word or block it. Blocked words are later remembered worse than words never cued. Niczyporuk calls this suppression-induced forgetting. Unlike the bear rebound, she writes, it replicates reliably. Distressing memories remain an open question For now the full paper sits behind a paywall, and its abstract gives neither the sample size nor the exact target thoughts. Niczyporuk’s review limits its verdict on effectiveness to healthy people. It adds that clinical groups appear to have a more limited capacity to use suppression effectively, so long-running anxiety and intrusive memories remain a separate question. Even in her own review, Niczyporuk stays careful about the takeaway. Suppression “may be adaptive, depending on factors such as individual differences and context,” she writes. That leaves room for both help and harm. The full study was published in Consciousness and Cognition . Photograph: Haven Daley/AP US news Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division Tom Perkins Fri 27 Nov 2026 10.00 EST Last modified on Fri 27 Nov 2026 10.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradicts a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weed killer is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup producer Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generates new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. If the EPA again finds that glyphosate is not carcinogenic, the NIH studies would complicate the legal terrain for it and Bayer. The papers also represent a major public relations hit for Bayer, which has relentlessly defended the herbicide, for which it recorded $2.8bn in sales in 2024. Nathan Donley, environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the studies raise further questions about chemical companies’ influence on the EPA’s pesticide division , which “parrots industry talking points” in its safety reviews. “Americans would be smart to heed the cancer findings of the nation’s most trusted scientific institution rather than the industry-influenced claims of the EPA,” Donley said. “The EPA’s pesticide office has made a mockery of pesticide science for far too long.” The EPA did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Ruveon, a Bayer subsidiary that manages Roundup in the US, said in a statement: “The US EPA, like other leading health authorities globally, has previously and repeatedly concluded that glyphosate does not cause cancer.” The NIH findings arrive during a year in which the White House has come under fire from across the political spectrum for its support for Bayer. That includes an executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to protect the substance’s production and provide immunity to its producers, and an amicus brief in support of Bayer in an eventual US supreme court case that partially shielded the company from lawsuits. The NIH did not carry out new studies, but conducted a systematic review of decades of scientific literature from across the globe. It found an association with blood cancers in humans, and that the pesticide caused several types of tumors in animals. Advocates say the NIH used proper scientific protocol, which is followed by the World Health Organization’s International Agency on Research for Cancer (IARC), and other credible research organizations. The EPA’s pesticide division reviewed most of the same studies several years ago but came to a different conclusion because it deviated from its own methodology, Donley said. A court threw out the EPA’s findings in 2022 because it did not use proper protocol, and ordered a new risk assessment. The EPA is expected to finish it early next year, Donley said. The EPA and NIH are often aligned on many chemicals’ risk assessments, but the pesticide division chronically underestimates cancer risks because of its flawed methodology, he added. “This agency is completely incapable of doing a good, clear, robust cancer assessment, not just with glyphosate, but all pesticides, because they don’t follow their own methodology,” Donley said. The administration’s support for glyphosate has driven a wedge between pro-industry figures in the White House, and the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, which health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr spearheads. Kelly Ryerson, a Maha advocate who has met with top agency officials to advocate for stricter pesticide policies, told the Guardian she is “extremely hopeful that glyphosate’s day of reckoning has arrived”. “The release of the government-performed studies on glyphosate further prove what many independent scientists have claimed for decades: glyphosate can cause cancer. The EPA will be forced to change its determination of carcinogenicity in the upcoming review,” Ryerson said. She noted the NIH papers are in addition to a recent US Department of Health and Human Services-commissioned study that similarly reviewed literature on glyphosate’s impact on hormones and found it likely reduced sperm counts and testosterone. Donley said he is “99.9% certain the EPA is going to again find that glyphosate does not cause cancer”. “They cannot possibly get their head around any other option, so they’re going to come out with that, then they’re going to get sued, and they’re going to get their behinds handed to them in court, again,” Donley said.
